blocks.content: 1.1 Ancient History

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Traces the historical timeline of Chhattisgarh from Ancient and Medieval periods to Maratha and British rule.
Explores key ancient sites and medieval dynasties that shaped the cultural heritage of the region.
Examines the origin and derivation of the name 'Chhattisgarh' alongside Maratha administration.
Highlights major revolts, freedom struggle figures, and crucial events leading to post-independence state formation.

blocks.content: Chhattisgarh, known as the 'Rice Bowl of Central India', has a rich ancient history dating back to the prehistoric era. The region finds mention in ancient Hindu texts, including the Ramayana and Mahabharata. The area was known as 'Dakshina Kosala' in ancient times.

Archaeological excavations have revealed evidence of human settlements from the Palaeolithic and Mesolithic periods. Rock paintings at Singanpur near Raigarh and Kabra Pahar near Raipur are among the oldest evidence of prehistoric human activity in the region.

The region was part of the Mauryan Empire during the reign of Emperor Ashoka (3rd century BCE). The spread of Buddhism in the region during this period is evidenced by the Buddhist stupas and viharas found at Sirpur, which was once an important Buddhist center.
Important Ancient Sites

cells: Temples of Ganeshas; ancient Chindak Nagvanshi capital
Kuleshwar Mahadev Temple; ancient temples on river confluence

blocks.content: 1.2 Medieval History

The medieval period in Chhattisgarh was dominated by various dynasties including the Sharabpuriya dynasty, Pandu dynasty, Soma dynasty, Kalachuri dynasty, and the Nagvanshi dynasty. The Kalachuris of Tripuri ruled from the 10th to 14th century CE and their influence spread across the Chhattisgarh region.

The Ratanpur branch of the Kalachuri dynasty established its capital at Ratanpur (near present-day Bilaspur). The Raipur branch of the same dynasty ruled from Raipur. This period witnessed significant temple construction and cultural development.
The Nagvanshi dynasty ruled over the Chhota Nagpur area and parts of present-day Chhattisgarh. They maintained a distinct tribal identity while also adopting elements of mainstream Hindu culture.

1.3 Maratha Rule in Chhattisgarh

After the decline of the Kalachuri dynasty, the Marathas extended their control over Chhattisgarh in the 18th century. The Bhonsle rulers of Nagpur established suzerainty over most of Chhattisgarh from around 1741 CE. They appointed a Subhedar (governor) to administer the region from Raipur.

Bimba Ji Bhonsle was the first Maratha Subhedar of Chhattisgarh. During the Maratha period, Chhattisgarh was administratively divided into 18 garhs (forts), each further divided into 5 chaukis. This administrative structure of 18 garhs is believed to be the origin of the name 'Chhattisgarh' (meaning 36 garhs or forts).
Derivation of the Name 'Chhattisgarh'

The name 'Chhattisgarh' literally means '36 forts'. According to historical accounts, the region was divided into 36 garhs (administrative units) during medieval times. The 18 garhs of Ratanpur and 18 garhs of Raipur together made 36 garhs, thus giving the name 'Chhattisgarh'. Another theory suggests that the word comes from 'Chhattisa Garh', referring to the 36 forts of the Kalachuri dynasty.
1.4 British Rule & Freedom Struggle

The British East India Company gained control over Chhattisgarh in 1818 CE following the defeat of the Marathas. The British appointed an administrative officer (Superintendent) to manage the region. Chhattisgarh was initially placed under the Bengal Presidency and later under the Central Provinces.

blocks.content: 1.5 Post-Independence & Formation of Chhattisgarh State

After India's independence in 1947, Chhattisgarh remained part of the Central Provinces and later the state of Madhya Pradesh formed in 1956. The demand for a separate Chhattisgarh state grew over decades due to the region's distinct cultural identity, language, and economic underdevelopment.

The demand for a separate state was consistently raised by various political leaders and organizations. The Chhattisgarh Rajya Nirman Manch (Chhattisgarh State Formation Forum) played a key role in mobilizing public opinion. After years of political advocacy, the Parliament of India passed the Madhya Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2000, which led to the creation of Chhattisgarh as the 26th state of India on November 1, 2000.
